claims.text: Low-temperature aging after homogenization can induce fine, dispersed precipitates in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
This aging treatment can simultaneously increase strength and ductility relative to the as-cast state.
The initial as-cast alloy has a coarse eutectic microstructure with limited precipitate refinement.
Aging at approximately 500°C for approximately 4 hours after homogenization will induce nanoprecipitation.
The aging temperature should remain below the eutectic decomposition threshold.
The proposed effect should hold in alloys with eutectic compositions similar to those studied.
Prior mechanical deformation could obscure aging-induced microstructural evolution.
The treatment forms a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates within the eutectic matrix.
The nanoscale precipitates improve dislocation pinning.
The treatment preserves an interconnected ductile-phase network.
Precipitates increase yield strength by impeding dislocation motion through precipitation strengthening.
An interconnected ductile phase improves strain distribution and thereby enhances ductility.
The treated alloy will have approximately 10–20% higher yield strength than the as-cast baseline.
The treated alloy will have approximately 10–20% higher elongation to failure than the as-cast baseline.
Different alloy systems or processing histories may produce different or adverse outcomes.
Minor changes in alloy chemistry may alter the optimum aging temperature, aging duration, and precipitate scale.

contradictions.description: The treated group receives both homogenization and aging, while the control remains untreated in the as-cast state. Thus, the experiment cannot isolate aging as the single causal intervention, because any observed difference could result from homogenization, aging, or their combination.
